items.title: OpenAI warns that upcoming AI systems could outpace safety checks and urges rivals to agree on shared limits
items.desc: OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki has released internal perplexity scores for the entire GPT series for the first time, up to an unreleased model beyond the current generation. The metric shows that core capabilities emerge at surprisingly precise thresholds. Pachocki is pushing to make perplexity an industry-wide progress metric and establish shared limits before control over AI behavior erodes. The article OpenAI warns that upcoming AI systems could outpace safety checks and urges rivals to agree on shared limits appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: OpenAI ties capabilities like fluent conversation and math breakthroughs to specific scores. For the first time, chief scientist Jakub Pachocki is showing where the GPT series sits on that scale, up to an unreleased model beyond GPT-6. Pachocki wants to make perplexity a common measure of progress for the AI industry and published internal scores for the GPT series in a bl o g post . The metric has long been standard in AI research and Transformer development because it reliably measures how well a pretrained base model predicts the next token in a text. Lower scores mean more accurate predictions. A perplexity of 2 roughly means the model is as uncertain about the next token as if it were choosing between two equally likely options. Before it stopped publishing openly, OpenAI often released perplexity scores to show how its models were improving. Releasing them again is a trade-off, Pachocki writes . While rivals get a clearer picture of where OpenAI stands, he says, the need for shared safety standards outweighs that downside. He hopes for a common scientific foundation that lets labs coordinate their pace of development at critical points. Pachocki says many capabilities of modern models map surprisingly closely to specific perplexity scores, even though it wasn't clear beforehand that they would appear at those thresholds. He reports the figures on a logarithmic scale called log-perplexity, where lower scores are still better. In his account, GPT-3.5 first enabled fluent conversation at around 0.99, laying the groundwork for the original ChatGPT. At about 0.91, GPT-4 unlocked productive chain-of-thought reasoning, or working through problems step by step. Below 0.8, he writes, transformative capabilities emerged in cybersecurity and math . The published chart plots OpenAI's base-model log-perplexity by release or evaluation date through November 2026. It covers GPT-5 , GPT-5.1 , GPT-5.2 , GPT-5.3-Codex , GPT-5.4 , GPT-5.5 , GPT-5.6 Sol , GPT-6 Astra , and GPT-6.2 Astra , plus an internal model at around 0.73. OpenAI has been feeding its models open math problems for more than a year. Starting with a model at about 0.76 log-perplexity, the models began producing breakthrough results, Pachocki writes. For researchers with a math background, he says, it was "deeply surreal" to watch solutions to longstanding questions pop up one after another in a single Slack thread. Those results include a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem , one of the Millennium Prize problems, though it hasn't been fully verified yet. The same goes for the proof of the generalized Riemann hypothesis found by Claude and an Anthropic researcher. Pachocki thinks deep learning research itself could see something similar as soon as 2027, bringing a sudden avalanche of core advances in AI training. A footnote says the sharp acceleration in the chart starting in 2026 comes mostly from long-term research and compute investments and less from automation. Even so, AI itself has contributed major design work on OpenAI's latest models, according to the post. items.title: Novartis CEO says AI will shave four years off drug development, not cure all disease
items.desc: Novartis CEO Vas Narasimhan, who also sits on Anthropic's board, is pushing back on the cure-all promises from Anthropic CEO Amodei and DeepMind founder Hassabis. AI will speed up drug development, he says, but it won't beat cancer in a decade. The real value lies "somewhere in the middle." The article Novartis CEO says AI will shave four years off drug development, not cure all disease appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Vas Narasimhan, CEO of Swiss drugmaker Novartis and an Anthropic board member, is pushing back on expectations that AI could cure cancer in five to 10 years. That puts him at odds with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and chemistry Nobel laureate Demis Hassabis , who founded DeepMind and its drug discovery spinoff Isomorphic. Around Anthropic's IPO , Amodei suggested that cancer, Alzheimer's, heart disease, and mental illness could be cured in under a decade, while Hassabis said last year that AI could defeat all diseases within 10 years. According to the Financial Times , Narasimhan points to a limited understanding of human biology, which is why lengthy animal and human trials will still be needed. His forecast is more cautious: within a decade, he expects AI to cut average drug development only from 12 years to eight, with the early phase before human trials alone accounting for up to two years of that. He also expects success rates in clinical development to rise from 8 percent to 12 percent. Anthropic is investing in its own drug research , acquired biotech startup Coefficient Bio, and is building a biology lab. Isomorphic raised $5 billion last week and is working with pharmaceutical companies including Novartis on new drugs. Narasimhan sees AI's real benefit as "somewhere in the middle" between ambitious AI forecasts and a skeptical pharma industry. Ad Ad Already a subscriber? Sign in

items.full: I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months. Here’s the video of the talk. In this post I’m going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply. Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5 . With hindsight, this was a consequential model. In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said: Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach. Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025. Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn’t been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn’t feel reliable enough—I had to correct it often enough that it didn’t feel like a clear accelerant. The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right . It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself. Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks. The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work. We got our first hint of Claude Fable in April, when Anthropic announced Claude Mythos and said that it was too dangerous to release , due to its improved cybersecurity capabilities. Mythos was a model that could not just find security vulnerabilities, it could also figure out how to exploit them. In June we got to see how good that model was for ourselves, with the release of Claude Fable 5—a defanged Mythos, that would solve most problems but would actively block you from using it for security work. After three glorious days... the US government took it away from us. Fable 5 was placed under export controls that effectively banned the model. We wouldn’t get it back until July 1st. For me, Fable was an inflection point because it introduced us to what I now think of as Fable class models . My definition of these: In June I wrote about how Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive , after I asked it to help fix a display glitch in Safari and it spun up its own pyobjc-framework-Quartz screenshot mechanism and a CORS-enabled localhost logging server to help resolve the bug. A more recent example of the power of Fable class models is my mysterious beep finder from a couple of weeks ago. items.title: MIT team discovers that unrealistic training data makes AI climate predictions more reliable
items.desc: MIT researchers have developed a method that lets AI climate models get by with a single training run instead of the usual six to eight. An algorithm generates deliberately unrealistic scenarios with extreme CO2 or methane swings that make the model more robust. Until now, these emulators were often outdated by the time they were finished, according to the researchers. The article MIT team discovers that unrealistic training data makes AI climate predictions more reliable appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: MIT researchers have developed a method that makes training AI climate models faster, cheaper, and more reliable. According to MIT News , these emulators now need only a fraction of the data typically required. Normally, researchers rely on massive, physics-based climate simulations that take months to run a single scenario on supercomputers. Fast AI models for climate prediction can mimic these in seconds and help plan power grids, public health measures, and agriculture. But training them previously required six to eight runs of those large simulations using evenly distributed, realistic future scenarios. That took so long the finished models were usually outdated, according to co-author Noelle Selin. They also often failed on unfamiliar situations. An algorithm built by a team from MIT, ETH Zurich, and Imperial College London uses synthetic training data with extreme swings instead, like a sudden CO2 spike in 2050 or dropping methane in 2037. These targeted spikes help the AI understand the climate system far more precisely, according to lead author Christopher Womack. A single simulation run is enough for training, according to the team, and the AI reliably calculates the effects of local environmental policies too. Ad Ad Already a subscriber? Sign in

items.title: PrismML shrinks a 54 GB language model to 5.9 GB by reducing every weight to just three possible values
items.desc: Startup PrismML has released Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B, an updated version of its aggressively compressed language model. The article PrismML shrinks a 54 GB language model to 5.9 GB by reducing every weight to just three possible values appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Startup PrismML has released Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B, an updated version of its aggressively compressed language model. It's based on Qwen3.8-27B and takes up just 5.9 GB of memory, same as its predecessor. That's possible because of ternary quantization, where each weight can only be one of three values (−1, 0, or +1) instead of the usual 16-bit storage. At full precision, a model this size would need about 54 GB. Bonsai 2.5 is designed to perform more reliably on agentic tasks that involve long chains of tool calls. It needs fewer passes and tokens than Bonsai 2, and it's less likely to get stuck in loops or spiral into drawn-out reasoning phases. The benchmark numbers reflect the improvement. On SWE-bench Verified, the score jumps from 60.8 to 75.6 percent. The full Qwen model hits 80.6. On AppWorld, an agent benchmark, Bonsai leaps from 51.2 to 90.5, landing just behind the base model. On LiveCodeBench v6, the new version scores slightly lower than its predecessor. Ad On an RTX 4090, the model generates about 204 tokens per second using multi-token prediction. The weights are available under an Apache 2.0 license and run via llama.cpp on Nvidia and Intel GPUs, as well as through MLX on Mac, iPhone, and iPad. PrismML grew out of a research team at Caltech and is backed by Khosla Ventures, Google, and Samsung, among others. The company first introduced Bonsai 27B in July , built on an older Qwen model. Its smallest variant needed less than 4 GB of memory, small enough to run directly on an iPhone. Already a subscriber? Sign in

items.title: AI agents now control part of Deepmind's compute for Gemini experiments, but recursive self-improvement remains distant
items.desc: Google Deepmind uses AI agents to run experiments on their own for upcoming Gemini models. Research chief Koray Kavukcuoglu says the lab is still far from recursive self-improvement. For oversight, Deepmind intentionally leaves the agents' internal chains of thought untrained so they can be reviewed. Kavukcuoglu measures AGI by everyday user trust rather than benchmarks. The article AI agents now control part of Deepmind's compute for Gemini experiments, but recursive self-improvement remains distant appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Google Deepmind lets AI agents run experiments on their own for the next Gemini model. On the company's podcast, VP of Research Koray Kavukcuoglu, who leads Gemini development, frames this as part of a strategic shift at the lab. Rather than running separate teams for specialized projects like AlphaFold and nuclear fusion, Deepmind now relies on a single general-purpose algorithm for both science and products, he says. Each Gemini generation, he adds, is a hand-built one-off rather than a fixed architecture, while parallel teams work on its successors. According to Kavukcuoglu, AI agents control part of the compute themselves to run experiments, though the lab is still far from full recursive self-improvement. As a safety measure, Deepmind doesn't reward the agents' internal thought streams ("Chain of Thought") during training, he says, so their intentions stay unfiltered and reviewable in natural language before they act. Kavukcuoglu also points to limits. Today's AI can depict physical processes such as fluid flows and collisions with visual accuracy, he says, but doesn't understand them precisely. No test can show when models will close those gaps and reach artificial general intelligence (AGI), he argues, because no benchmark captures the core of intelligence. In his view, AGI won't begin until useful everyday products earn enough trust for people to hand decisions over to them, the way they would when working with other people. Ad Ad Already a subscriber? The course is 32% off until December 2, 2026. Modifiers have been with us for a long time, often with modifier classes, but also with attribute selectors. Some common examples are things like different versions of alerts and buttons. /* BEM approach */ .button--accent { background-color: var(--clr-accent); } /* CUBECSS approach */ .toast[data-type="error"] { border-color: var(--clr-warning); } For a lot of use cases, either of those approaches work great, but when it comes to layout, a lot of the time we want the context of where the element is being used to control things. A card is a nice example of this, where we might have several versions. .card { display: grid; gap: .75rem; } .card--horizontal { grid-template-columns: 1fr 2fr; } .card--compact { padding: .75rem; gap: .5rem; } The issue here is, if I’m using .card--compact , I probably want to do that for all the cards within a section. That can be annoying to apply to each card, but that’s rendered moot since most people are doing some sort of looping in a template like this these days.

And this works great, as long as we always want the cards to be compact. However, you might put this together and send it off to the design team for approval, only for them not to like that when the compact cards are lower down the page, the smaller padding isn’t needed to create visual separation between the two sections. Instead of helping with the hierarchy, it’s simply creating a strange visual inconsistency. We could use something like a resize observer to try and deal with this, but we have a better tool at our disposal: Container Style Queries , which are now Baseline Newly Available . While they all start with container , for the rest of this article I interchangeable use container query or size query for a container size query, and style query for what we’re talking about here. A quick look at style queries Before we get into the good stuff, a quick look at the basics of style queries. You’re probably familiar with size queries, which work similar to @media but look at the size of a container, rather than the viewport. Container style queries use the same @container at-rule as container size queries, but instead of looking at a size, they look at the value of a custom property. @container style(--theme: high-contrast) { .card { background: white; color: black; border-color: black; } } This reads as, “if the nearest container has --theme: high-contrast , style the .card like this.” A couple of important notes about them: Elements can’t query themselves Just like with size queries, style queries look at an ancestor , not the element itself.
